words: carrying capacity; limiting factor; population; density-dependent; density-independent; model run
cross_subject: math:S-ID.B.6 (fit a function to population data over time); math:N-Q.A.2 (define the quantities a population model tracks)
notes: Explain why a population levels off, crashes or grows by using graphs and a simple computational model (a spreadsheet or a provided simulation) of births, deaths and resources. Factors compared: space and boundaries, food and water, climate, competition, predation; at more than one scale (a pond, a park, a region). The grade 7 food web and population ideas become quantitative: students change one input and predict the curve before running it. Introduces computational-model (a model that steps quantities forward by rules), used again in chemistry and physics. Limit (assessment boundary): students do not derive the equations; they use and adjust given ones.

words: biodiversity; species richness; abundance; sample; mean; trend
cross_subject: math:S-ID.A.2 (compare centre and spread of two data sets)
notes: Use averages, trends and side-by-side graphs of provided survey data (quadrat counts, bird counts, fishery records) to support and then revise an explanation of what changed biodiversity or a population in an ecosystem. The growth from middle school is revision: a second data set arrives and the class changes its explanation. Limit: provided data only (assessment boundary); no diversity index formulas required.

words: stability; disturbance; resilience; succession; equilibrium; new ecosystem
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (evaluate the argument and evidence in a text)
notes: Evaluate claims, evidence and reasoning that an ecosystem keeps similar numbers and kinds of organisms while conditions are stable, and that a large change (sea level rise, a volcanic eruption) can produce a different ecosystem, while a modest one (a seasonal flood, moderate hunting) is absorbed. Crosscutting concept: stability and change. Students judge whether an argument's evidence covers the scale of change it claims.

words: group behaviour; flocking; schooling; cooperation; survival; reproduction
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (judge whether the evidence is relevant and sufficient)
notes: Evaluate evidence that group behaviour (flocking, schooling, herding, cooperative hunting, social insect colonies) changes an individual's and a species' chances to survive and reproduce. Students weigh study designs: what was measured, compared with what, and whether the evidence separates the group effect from other causes. Short skill, usually one section inside the ecosystems unit.

words: criteria; constraint; trade-off; invasive species; habitat loss; mitigation
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.1 (units in quantitative criteria such as hectares or cost per year)
notes: Engineering first done in full here (HS-ETS1-1 is owned by this row and used again in chemistry and physics). Students analyse a large human impact on biodiversity (urban growth, a dam, an invasive species), state qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints that account for what people need and want, then design, evaluate and refine a solution that reduces the impact (HS-LS2-7). The grade 8 design cycle grows by adding numbers to criteria and by naming whose needs a constraint protects.

words: technological solution; prioritise; trade-off; reliability; impact data; pollutant
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.3 (judge the precision of impact data used to compare solutions)
notes: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces human impact on natural systems (HS-ESS3-4, core idea ESS3.C, placed in Biology as NGSS Appendix K places it) using impact data (pollutant amounts, biomass and species diversity, land use change), and judge it against prioritised criteria and trade-offs: cost, safety, reliability, looks, and social, cultural and environmental effects (HS-ETS1-3, first done in full here, used again in chemistry and physics). Range from local (reuse and recycling) to large scale (geoengineering proposals), weighed on evidence, not on opinion.

words: photosynthesis; glucose; chloroplast; chemical energy; light energy; reactant; product
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.A.1 (read the parts of a balanced equation as counts of molecules)
notes: Use a model (diagram, balanced equation, conceptual model) to show how photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water and, with light energy, makes sugar and oxygen, so light energy becomes chemical energy stored in the products. Builds on grade 7 photosynthesis by tracking atoms and energy separately and accounting for both. Limit: no light reactions, Calvin cycle or other biochemical steps (assessment boundary).

words: cellular respiration; aerobic; anaerobic; fermentation; bond; net energy transfer
notes: Model cellular respiration as a chemical process: bonds in food molecules and oxygen break, bonds in carbon dioxide and water form, and the difference is a net release of energy the cell uses (HS-LS1-7). Then explain, with evidence, how matter cycles and energy flows when oxygen is present and when it is not, in places such as waterlogged soil, muscle in hard exercise and bread dough (HS-LS2-3). Bond energy stays qualitative here; chemistry makes it a model of total bond energy. Limit: no steps of glycolysis or the Krebs cycle, no specific chemical processes (both assessment boundaries). Teacher note: yeast and dough investigations use warm water only, no flames.

words: amino acid; protein; carbon-based molecule; sugar; element; large molecule
notes: Construct and revise an explanation, from models and simulations, of how the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in sugar from photosynthesis combine with other elements (such as nitrogen and sulfur) to build amino acids and other large carbon-based molecules. Links the matter story (where does a tree's mass come from) to growth. Limit: no details of the specific reactions and no identifying macromolecules by name as the goal (assessment boundary).

words: trophic level; biomass; energy pyramid; producer; consumer; conservation of matter
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent of stored energy passed from one trophic level to the next)
notes: Use a mathematical model of stored energy in biomass to show how energy passes from one trophic level to the next (roughly a tenth carried up, the rest released as heat by respiration), and that carbon, oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen atoms are conserved as matter cycles. Grows the grade 7 food web into proportional accounting. Limit: proportional reasoning only (assessment boundary).

words: carbon cycle; biosphere; atmosphere; hydrosphere; geosphere; reservoir; flux
notes: Develop a model of how photosynthesis and cellular respiration move carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere (models may be diagrams, simulations or simple mathematical models). Students mark which arrows are biological and which are not, and where carbon is stored for a long time. Hands the matter-cycle model to chemistry, which makes the whole carbon cycle quantitative (HS-ESS2-6). Limit: no chemical steps of photosynthesis or respiration (assessment boundary).

words: cell; tissue; organ; organ system; hierarchy; interacting systems
notes: Develop and use a model of the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism (cells, tissues, organs, organ systems) and how systems interact to do whole-organism jobs: taking in nutrients, delivering water, moving in response to a nerve signal. Example: an artery depends on elastic tissue and smooth muscle to deliver the right amount of blood. Grows the grade 6 cell and body systems unit into interacting levels. Limit: nothing at the molecular or chemical reaction level (assessment boundary).

words: homeostasis; feedback; negative feedback; set point; stimulus; response
cross_subject: math:S-ID.A.1 (plot and compare repeated measurements)
notes: Plan and conduct an investigation that gives evidence of feedback keeping a condition steady: heart rate and recovery after exercise, stomata opening with moisture and temperature, root growth toward water. Students choose what to vary and hold steady and read the data for a return toward a set point. Limit: not the cellular processes inside the feedback (assessment boundary). Teacher note: exercise investigations are voluntary and light, with a seated alternative and no student required to share personal health data; students with a medical reason take the data-recording role or use a class data set.

words: DNA; gene; protein; base sequence; code; specialised cell
notes: Construct an explanation from evidence of how the order of bases in DNA sets the order of amino acids in a protein, and how proteins do the work of life in systems of specialised cells. Builds on the grade 8 gene to protein to trait idea with the structure of DNA as the reason. Limit: no naming of specific cell or tissue types, whole body systems, specific protein structures, or the biochemistry of transcription and translation (assessment boundary).

words: mitosis; cell division; differentiation; stem cell; growth; repair
notes: Use a model to show how cell division (mitosis) copies a cell's DNA into two cells, and how differentiation lets cells with the same DNA become different kinds, so an organism grows, repairs itself and stays complex. Limit: no specific gene control mechanisms and no memorising the phases of mitosis (assessment boundary).

words: chromosome; allele; inherit; trait; non-coding DNA; parent; offspring
notes: Ask questions that clarify how DNA and chromosomes carry the instructions for traits passed from parents to offspring, including that not all DNA codes for proteins and that some segments have regulatory or unknown jobs. The practice is asking good questions: students sort questions that can be tested, refine vague ones, and say what evidence would answer them. Limit: no phases of meiosis or biochemical mechanisms (assessment boundary).

words: meiosis; recombination; mutation; replication error; mutagen; heritable variation
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.1 (write an argument with a claim backed by evidence)
notes: Make and defend a claim, from data, that heritable variation comes from new combinations of genes in meiosis, from viable errors when DNA is copied, and from mutations caused by environmental factors (ultraviolet light, some chemicals). Hands on to physics the idea that radiation can change DNA. Limit: no phases of meiosis (assessment boundary). Teacher note: if cancer or a genetic condition is used as a case, keep it general, avoid asking about family illness, and give students who are affected a quiet way out of the discussion.

words: probability; distribution; genotype; phenotype; dominant; recessive; environment
cross_subject: math:7.SP.C.8 (probabilities of compound events for crosses); math:S-ID.A.1 (plot the distribution of a trait)
notes: Apply probability and simple statistics to explain the variation and distribution of traits in a population: expected ratios from crosses, distributions of measured traits, and how genes and environment both shape what is expressed. Limit: no Hardy-Weinberg calculations (assessment boundary). Teacher note: use plant, animal or class-invented traits, never students' own family traits or ancestry.

words: common ancestry; evolution; homologous structure; DNA sequence; embryo; fossil record; line of evidence
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.2 (write an explanatory text that conveys complex ideas clearly)
notes: Communicate (in writing, graphics and talk) how several independent lines of evidence (similar DNA sequences, shared anatomical structures, the order structures appear in embryo development, the fossil record) each support common ancestry and biological evolution, and why agreement among them is strong. Grows the grade 8 natural selection and common ancestry unit with molecular evidence. Teacher note: evolution is taught as the evidence shows, without softening (BASELINE rule 5); respect students' beliefs while keeping the science claims clear.

words: natural selection; adaptation; variation; competition; reproductive success; gene frequency
notes: Construct an explanation from evidence that evolution results mainly from four factors: populations can grow, individuals vary heritably through mutation and sexual reproduction, resources are limited so there is competition, and those better able to survive and reproduce leave more offspring (HS-LS4-2). Then explain how natural selection leads to adaptation of a population, using data on how biotic and abiotic differences (temperature range, climate change, acidity, light, geographic barriers, other species) change gene frequency over time (HS-LS4-4). Limit: genetic drift, gene flow and co-evolution are not required (assessment boundary of HS-LS4-2).

words: proportion; advantageous trait; generation; frequency; histogram; shift
cross_subject: math:S-ID.A.1 (histograms of a trait across generations); math:S-ID.A.3 (interpret a shift in centre and shape)
notes: Apply statistics and probability to show that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion over generations: compare distributions of a trait before and after a selection pressure and use the shift as evidence. Limit: basic statistical and graphical analysis only, no allele frequency calculations (assessment boundary).

words: speciation; extinction; reproductive isolation; rate of change; habitat; geographic barrier
notes: Evaluate evidence for claims that changes in the environment can increase some species' numbers, lead to new species over time, and cause others to go extinct. Cause and effect at different rates: deforestation, fishing, fertiliser runoff, drought, flood, and slow changes such as a moving continent or rising mountain range separating populations (the plate-model, carried from grade 6 so physics can use it in grade 11). Students judge which claims the evidence supports and which it does not.

words: simulation; parameter; sustainability; endangered species; resource management; scenario
cross_subject: math:F-BF.A.1 (write a rule for how a quantity changes each step); math:S-ID.B.6 (compare model output with real data)
notes: Use and revise a computer simulation to test solutions for a problem with many criteria and constraints. Three standards together: create or revise a simulation to test a way to lessen human harm to an endangered species or to genetic variation (HS-LS4-6); create a computational simulation of how managing a natural resource (harvest, extraction cost, per-person use, new technology, urban planning) affects human sustainability and biodiversity (HS-ESS3-3, placed in Biology as Appendix K places it); and use the simulation to model the effect of proposed solutions on interactions within and between systems (HS-ETS1-4, first done in full here, used again in chemistry and physics). Limit: provided multi-parameter programs or simplified spreadsheet calculations (assessment boundary of HS-ESS3-3).

words: coevolution; biosphere; oxygenation; weathering; soil formation; reef; feedback
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.1 (argument from evidence)
notes: Construct an argument from evidence that Earth's systems and life have changed each other at the same time: photosynthetic life put oxygen in the air, which sped weathering and made animal life possible; microbes on land made soil, which let land plants evolve; corals built reefs that changed erosion and gave homes to new life. Placed in Biology as NGSS Appendix K and the high school reference units both do; it closes the evolution unit and hands the idea of feedback between Earth systems to chemistry. Limit: not a full account of how the biosphere interacts with every Earth system (assessment boundary).

words: atom; nucleus; proton; neutron; electron; valence electron; periodic table; group; period; reactivity
notes: Use the periodic table as a model to predict relative properties of main group elements from the pattern of electrons in the outermost energy level: reactivity of metals, kinds and numbers of bonds formed, reactions with oxygen. Grows the grade 7 particle model (atoms and molecules) into atoms with inner structure. Introduces periodic-table (a new model name: the table read as a model of electron patterns, not a list). Limit: main group elements only; ionization energy as relative trends only (assessment boundary).

words: intermolecular attraction; melting point; boiling point; surface tension; vapour pressure; electric force; network solid
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.3 (precision of measured melting and boiling temperatures)
notes: Plan and conduct an investigation comparing bulk properties of substances (melting and boiling point, vapour pressure, surface tension) to infer how strong the electrical attractions between their particles are, for ions, atoms, molecules and network materials such as graphite. Introduces electric force between charged particles qualitatively; physics makes it Coulomb's law. Limit: strength of forces, not names of intermolecular forces; no Raoult's law (clarification and boundary). Teacher note: heating uses hot plates or warm water baths, never open flames with flammable liquids; eye protection; teacher-approved substances only.

words: polymer; conductor; designed material; molecular structure; receptor; attraction; repulsion
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.2 (communicate technical information clearly)
notes: Communicate scientific and technical information about why the molecular-level structure of a designed material makes it work: why conductors are usually metals, why long-chain molecules make flexible but tough materials, why a medicine fits a particular receptor. Placed in Chemistry, not Physics as NGSS Appendix K places it, because its core is the attractive and repulsive forces between particles that chem-bulk-properties-forces builds in the same course, as the high school reference units also place it. Limit: provided molecular structures only (assessment boundary).

words: polarity; solubility; weathering; erosion; deposition; frost wedging; melting point
notes: Plan and conduct mechanical and chemical investigations of how water's properties (it expands when it freezes, dissolves many solids, carries sediment, lowers the melting point of rock) shape Earth materials and surface processes: stream table erosion and deposition, frost wedging, solubility of different rocks, melting with water present. Connects the water cycle to the rock cycle, and gives the reason water helps melt rock where plates sink (the plate-model, carried to physics). water-cycle and rock-cycle come from grade 6 and 7 and are not used in grade 9: no biology standard calls for them. Placed in Chemistry as Appendix K places it. Teacher note: stream tables need drip trays and wiped floors; any acid test for carbonate rock uses dilute vinegar or teacher-prepared dilute acid with eye protection.

words: chemical reaction; ionic bond; covalent bond; combustion; electron transfer; product prediction
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.1 (construct and revise an explanation as a written argument)
notes: Construct and revise an explanation for the outcome of a simple reaction from outer electron states, periodic trends and patterns of chemical properties: sodium and chlorine, carbon and oxygen, carbon and hydrogen. Students predict the product, test the prediction with evidence, and revise. Limit: main group elements and combustion reactions only (assessment boundary). Teacher note: the sodium and chlorine reaction is shown by video or teacher description only, never done in a classroom.

words: conservation of mass; mole; molar mass; balanced equation; coefficient; proportion
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.1 (units guide the conversion between grams and moles); math:8.EE.A.4 (scientific notation for numbers of particles)
notes: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that atoms, and so mass, are conserved in a reaction, using the mole to move between the atomic scale and grams on a balance. Emphasis is mathematical thinking about proportions between masses of reactants and products, not memorised procedures. Grows the grade 7 conservation of atoms into quantities. Limit: no complex reactions (assessment boundary). Teacher note: closed-system mass investigations (for example baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bag) use small amounts; never seal a rigid container.

words: bond energy; endothermic; exothermic; energy diagram; reaction system; activation
notes: Develop a model (molecular drawings, energy diagrams of reactants and products, energy-conservation accounts) showing that whether a reaction system releases or absorbs energy depends on the change in total bond energy: breaking bonds takes energy, forming bonds releases it. Makes the grade 9 qualitative idea from cellular respiration and photosynthesis into a general model. Limit: no calculating total bond energy changes from tables (assessment boundary). Teacher note: hot and cold pack investigations use teacher-chosen salts with gloves and eye protection.

words: reaction rate; collision; concentration; temperature; kinetic energy; activation energy
cross_subject: math:S-ID.B.6 (plot rate against temperature or concentration)
notes: Apply scientific principles and evidence to explain how changing temperature or concentration changes the rate of a reaction, reasoning about how many collisions happen and with how much energy. Limit: simple two-reactant reactions; evidence from temperature, concentration and rate data; qualitative rate and temperature relations (assessment boundary). Teacher note: effervescent tablets in water or dilute vinegar with baking soda are the default; any acid is teacher-diluted, with eye protection.

words: equilibrium; reversible reaction; Le Chatelier's principle; yield; condition; product
notes: Refine the design of a chemical system by naming one change in conditions (add reactant, remove product, change temperature or pressure) that increases the amount of product at equilibrium, and connect the change at the large scale to what happens at the particle scale (Le Chatelier's principle). A design standard: criteria are yield and conditions a plant can afford. Limit: one variable at a time; no equilibrium constants or concentrations (assessment boundary).

words: thermal energy; temperature; heat transfer; thermal equilibrium; specific heat; second law of thermodynamics
cross_subject: math:A-CED.A.4 (rearrange the energy equation to find a final temperature)
notes: Plan and conduct an investigation (mixing water at different starting temperatures, adding a warm metal object to cool water) showing that thermal energy moves from hotter to colder parts of a closed system until energy is spread more evenly (the second law of thermodynamics). Describe the energy changes both in numbers and in words. Builds on grade 6 thermal energy. Limit: materials and tools provided to students (assessment boundary). Teacher note: water no hotter than a hot plate on low or a kettle poured by an adult; insulated cups; spills wiped at once.

words: energy conservation; system boundary; input; output; computational model; efficiency
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.A.1 (explain what each term in an energy expression means); math:A-CED.A.4 (solve for the unknown energy change)
notes: Create a computational model (spreadsheet or short program) that calculates the energy change of one part of a system when the changes of the other parts and the flows in and out are known, and explain what each expression in the model means. In Chemistry the systems are thermal and chemical (a calorimeter, a warming pond, Earth's surface energy budget); physics carries the same model to kinetic energy and energy in fields. Uses the grade 9 skill of stepping a quantity forward by rules in a computational model (bio-population-carrying-capacity), now with energy as the quantity. Placed in Chemistry as Appendix K places it. Limit: basic algebra; two or three components (assessment boundary).

words: energy conversion; prototype; efficiency; sub-problem; iterate; constraint
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.1 (compare total output with input in consistent units)
notes: Design, build and refine a device that converts one form of energy to another within constraints (a solar oven, a solar water heater, a chemical hand warmer, a simple turbine), judged on total output for a given input and on criteria such as renewable energy and efficiency (HS-PS3-3, placed in Chemistry as Appendix K places it). The device is designed by breaking the complex problem into smaller ones that can each be solved and tested (HS-ETS1-2, first done in full here, used again in physics). Uses criteria and trade-offs from grade 9. Limit: devices built from provided materials; quantitative evaluation only of total output for a given input (assessment boundary). Teacher note: solar ovens get hot; no glass that can shatter; hand warmers use iron powder kits, not homemade chemicals.

words: climate; energy budget; greenhouse gas; infrared radiation; albedo; orbit; timescale
notes: Use a model of energy flowing into and out of Earth's systems to explain how changes in that flow change climate, on different timescales: a large volcanic eruption or ocean circulation (1 to 10 years); human activity, solar output, ocean circulation (decades to centuries); changes in Earth's orbit and tilt (tens to hundreds of thousands of years); long-term changes in the atmosphere (millions of years). Carbon dioxide absorbing infrared light is the particle-level reason. wave-model (light) and earth-sun-moon (orbit and tilt) come from grade 8; no biology standard uses them in grade 9. Limit: effects only on surface temperature, precipitation, ice volume, sea level and where living things live (assessment boundary). Teacher note: climate change is taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5); end with what people are doing, so the topic is not only frightening.

words: feedback; positive feedback; albedo; runoff; groundwater; Earth system
cross_subject: math:S-ID.C.9 (correlation is not causation when reading linked data sets)
notes: Analyse geoscience data to claim that one change to Earth's surface can set off feedbacks that change other Earth systems: warming melts ice, which reflects less sunlight, which warms further; lost vegetation raises runoff and erosion; a dam raises groundwater, cuts sediment and increases coastal erosion. Placed in Chemistry, not Physics as NGSS Appendix K places it, because its required example is the climate feedback that chem-earth-energy-climate builds in the same course; the high school reference units also place it with climate in chemistry. Uses the grade 9 idea that life and Earth systems change each other.

words: carbon reservoir; flux; gigatonne; ocean uptake; fossil fuel; residence time
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.1 (units of carbon stocks and flows); math:F-BF.A.1 (a stock changes each year by inflow minus outflow)
notes: Develop a quantitative model of carbon cycling among the ocean, atmosphere, soil, rock and living things (including people), with reservoirs and yearly flows in numbers, and use it to explain why carbon dioxide in the air is rising. Turns the grade 9 biological carbon cycle into a full Earth-system stock and flow model, adding the chemistry of carbon dissolving in seawater and stored in rock and fuels.

words: forecast; climate model; projection; rate of change; uncertainty; sea level
cross_subject: math:S-ID.C.7 (interpret the slope of a trend as a rate); math:S-ID.B.6 (fit a trend to a time series)
notes: Analyse geoscience data and results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and one of its impacts (on sea level, ice volume, or the make-up of the air or ocean). Students separate measured data from model projections and state the range of the forecast. Limit: one example of a climate change and its impacts (assessment boundary). Teacher note: as for chem-earth-energy-climate; local impacts can touch students' homes and families, so keep the focus on evidence and on responses.

words: ocean acidification; pH; cryosphere; human activity; model output; Earth system interaction
notes: Use a computational representation to show how Earth systems (hydrosphere, atmosphere, cryosphere, geosphere, biosphere) are linked and how human activity is changing the links, for example more carbon dioxide raising plant growth on land and acidifying the ocean, with effects on shellfish and marine populations. Uses the grade 9 skill of reading and revising a simulation. Limit: students use published results of scientific models; they do not run the models (assessment boundary).

words: natural resource; natural hazard; fertile soil; groundwater; migration; settlement
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-geography-shapes-contact (grade 9 world history: human and physical systems shape each other)
notes: Construct an explanation from evidence of how the availability of resources (fresh water, fertile river deltas, minerals and fossil fuels), natural hazards (eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, droughts, hurricanes) and changes in climate (sea level, rainfall, which crops can grow) have shaped where and how people live, including mass migrations. Placed in Chemistry, not Biology as NGSS Appendix K places it, because it needs the climate change and resource ideas this course builds (the high school reference units also place it in chemistry). Teacher note: disasters and forced migration can be personal for some students; choose cases with care and give a quiet way out.

words: cost-benefit ratio; mineral resource; extraction; recycling; reuse; reclamation
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.2 (choose the quantities that make a fair cost-benefit comparison)
notes: Evaluate competing design solutions for developing, managing and using energy and mineral resources by cost-benefit ratio: farming soil practices, mining coal or oil sands, pumping oil and gas, recycling metals. Emphasis on conservation, recycling and reuse where possible and on keeping harm small where not. Science says what can happen in natural systems, not what should happen: students keep the two apart. Uses the grade 9 trade-off evaluation (bio-evaluate-impact-solutions).

words: nucleus; isotope; radioactive decay; alpha; beta; gamma; half-life; fission; fusion
cross_subject: math:F-LE.A.1c (half-life as decay by a constant percent per interval)
notes: Develop simple qualitative models (pictures, diagrams) of how the nucleus changes in fission, fusion and alpha, beta and gamma decay, and of how much more energy nuclear processes release than chemical ones (the scale comparison is the point). Half-life is modelled with dice or coins as a constant fraction lost per interval. Hands on to physics, where it explains the Sun, the making of elements in stars and radiometric dating of rocks. Limit: no calculation of energy released; only alpha, beta and gamma decay (assessment boundary). Teacher note: no radioactive sources in class; nuclear weapons and accidents may come up, so answer factually and briefly.

words: net force; acceleration; mass; velocity; Newton's second law; free-body diagram
cross_subject: math:F-IF.B.6 (slope of a velocity-time graph as acceleration); math:A-CED.A.2 (equation relating force, mass and acceleration)
notes: Analyse data (tables and graphs of position or velocity against time for a falling object, a cart on a ramp, an object pulled by a constant force) to support the claim that Newton's second law gives the relationship among net force, mass and acceleration. Grows the grade 8 contact forces unit into a quantitative law. force-diagram last used in grade 8; grades 9 and 10 do not use it because no biology or chemistry standard concerns forces on objects. Limit: one-dimensional motion, everyday speeds (assessment boundary).

words: momentum; collision; impulse; closed system; conservation; velocity
cross_subject: math:A-CED.A.4 (solve the momentum equation for an unknown velocity)
notes: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that the total momentum of a system of two objects stays the same when no net outside force acts, in numbers and in words. Limit: two objects in one dimension (assessment boundary).

words: impulse; collision time; crumple zone; prototype; test; refine
cross_subject: math:A-CED.A.4 (rearrange impulse to compare forces across collision times)
notes: Apply science and engineering ideas to design, evaluate and refine a device that lowers the force on an object in a collision (an egg-drop package, a helmet liner, a parachute): longer collision time means smaller force for the same change in momentum. Engineering practices from grades 9 and 10 (criteria and constraints, breaking the problem down, trade-offs, simulation) are used again here; the four HS-ETS1 standards are owned earlier and used in this course. Limit: qualitative evaluation and algebra (assessment boundary). Teacher note: drop tests from a fixed low height or a teacher-held point; no student climbs.

words: gravitational force; electric force; charge; inverse square; field; Coulomb's law
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.A.1 (interpret the inverse-square expression term by term)
notes: Use Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law to describe and predict gravitational and electric forces between two objects, in numbers and as fields. Makes quantitative the electric attraction between particles from grade 10 chemistry. Introduces field-model (a new model name: a field around a mass, charge or magnet that acts on another object at a distance); if the grade 6 to 8 writer hands on field-model from grade 8 forces at a distance, this row carries it instead (grades 9 and 10 would then not use it, since no biology or chemistry standard concerns fields). Limit: systems of two objects (assessment boundary).

words: orbit; satellite; ellipse; period; Kepler's laws; gravitational attraction
cross_subject: math:A-CED.A.4 (rearrange orbital relations to find a period or distance)
notes: Use mathematical or computational representations (a step-by-step spreadsheet orbit, Kepler's laws) to predict the motion of orbiting objects in the solar system: planets, moons and satellites people launch. Newton's law of gravitation is the reason. Limit: two bodies, no calculus (assessment boundary).

words: kinetic energy; potential energy; gravitational potential energy; field energy; thermal energy; energy conversion
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.A.1 (meaning of each term in kinetic and potential energy expressions)
notes: Develop and use models (diagrams, drawings, simulations) showing that energy at the everyday scale is a combination of energy of motion and energy of relative position: kinetic energy becoming thermal energy, energy stored by height above Earth, energy stored between charged plates. Extends the grade 10 energy-accounting model to kinetic energy and energy in fields.

words: electric field; magnetic field; attraction; repulsion; field energy; interaction
notes: Develop and use a model of two objects interacting through an electric or magnetic field to show the forces between them and how each object's energy changes as they move (for example two opposite charges pulled together lose field energy and gain kinetic energy). Limit: two objects (assessment boundary).

words: electric current; magnetic field; electromagnet; induction; generator; coil
notes: Plan and conduct an investigation giving evidence that an electric current makes a magnetic field (a compass near a wire, an electromagnet) and that a changing magnetic field makes a current (a magnet moved through a coil read on a meter). Leads to how generators supply electricity. Limit: investigations designed with provided materials and tools (assessment boundary). Teacher note: low-voltage batteries only; coils and wires can get hot when shorted, so short circuits are brief and supervised; never use mains power.

words: frequency; wavelength; wave speed; medium; period; seismic wave
cross_subject: math:A-CED.A.4 (rearrange speed equals frequency times wavelength)
notes: Use mathematical representations to support a claim about how frequency, wavelength and speed are related for waves in different media: light in a vacuum and in glass, sound in air and water, seismic waves through Earth. Grows the grade 8 sound and grade 6 light units into one wave relation. Limit: algebraic relationships and qualitative description (assessment boundary).

words: electromagnetic radiation; photon; interference; diffraction; photoelectric effect; wave model; particle model
cross_subject: ela:RI.11-12.8 (evaluate the reasoning and evidence behind a scientific claim)
notes: Evaluate the claims, evidence and reasoning that light can be described by a wave model or a particle model, and that for some cases one is more useful: interference and diffraction fit waves; the photoelectric effect fits particles. Emphasis on how evidence supports a claim and how a theory changes when new evidence arrives (nature of science taught on purpose here). Limit: no quantum theory (assessment boundary).

words: ultraviolet; X-ray; microwave; ionising radiation; photon energy; absorption; source reliability
cross_subject: ela:RI.11-12.8 (judge the validity and reliability of claims in published sources)
notes: Evaluate the validity and reliability of claims in published materials (articles, websites, videos that may show bias) about what different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation do when absorbed by matter: higher-frequency photons carry more energy, so ultraviolet and X-rays can damage living tissue and DNA while radio waves and visible light do not in the same way. Skips chemistry on purpose: the grade 9 idea that environmental factors such as ultraviolet light cause mutations (bio-sources-of-variation) is what this row uses, and no grade 10 standard covers DNA. Limit: qualitative only (assessment boundary). Teacher note: cell phone and wireless worries come up; weigh sources, do not mock.

words: digital signal; analog signal; bit; noise; storage; transmission
notes: Evaluate questions about the advantages of digital transmission and storage of information: it is stable, copies without loss, and moves and spreads quickly; against that, it can be deleted, stolen or kept insecurely. Students sharpen questions into ones that evidence can answer. Grows the grade 8 idea that digital signals are more reliable than analog.

words: solar cell; medical imaging; transmitter; receiver; signal; energy capture
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.2 (explanatory writing of technical information)
notes: Communicate technical information about how devices use wave behaviour and the way waves interact with matter to send and capture information and energy: solar cells turning light into electricity, medical imaging, communication technology. Limit: qualitative only; no band theory (assessment boundary).

words: nuclear fusion; core; radiation; sunspot; solar flare; star mass; lifespan
notes: Develop a model from evidence of the Sun's life span and how fusion in its core releases energy that reaches Earth as radiation: energy transfer outward from the core; evidence from masses and lifetimes of other stars, solar flares, the 11-year sunspot cycle and slower variations. Uses grade 10 fusion and the energy budget of Earth from grade 10 climate. Limit: no atomic and subatomic details of fusion (assessment boundary).

words: nucleosynthesis; element; star life cycle; supernova; heavy element; red giant
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.2 (communicate a scientific explanation)
notes: Communicate scientific ideas about how stars, over their lives, make elements, and how what a star makes depends on its mass and stage: hydrogen to helium, then heavier elements in massive stars, the heaviest in their explosions. Uses grade 10 fusion and the periodic table. Limit: not the details of the many nucleosynthesis pathways (assessment boundary).

words: Big Bang; redshift; spectrum; galaxy; cosmic microwave background; expanding universe
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.1 (argument from evidence)
notes: Construct an explanation of the Big Bang theory from astronomical evidence: redshift of light from galaxies shows the universe is expanding; the cosmic microwave background is left-over radiation; the measured make-up of ordinary matter (about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium, read from star spectra) matches the prediction. Uses wave behaviour from this course and the grade 10 idea that each element has its own electron arrangement.

words: mantle; core; convection; density; seismic wave; magnetic field; radioactive heat
notes: Develop a model based on evidence of Earth's interior to describe how thermal convection cycles matter: a layered model with layers set by density, and a three-dimensional model of mantle convection driving plate motion. Evidence: maps of Earth's interior from seismic waves (phys-wave-math), changes in Earth's magnetic field (constraints on outer-core convection), and high-pressure experiments on rock. Uses grade 10 thermal energy transfer.

words: orogeny; uplift; volcanism; trench; ridge; seamount; mass wasting; time scale
notes: Develop a model of how Earth's internal and surface processes, working at different spatial and time scales, form continental and ocean-floor features: building forces (volcanism, uplift, mountain building) against wearing-down ones (weathering, mass wasting, coastal erosion, from grade 10 water and Earth materials). Limit: not memorising how specific named features formed (assessment boundary).

words: oceanic crust; continental crust; mid-ocean ridge; sea-floor spreading; radiometric age; craton
cross_subject: math:S-ID.B.6 (age against distance from a ridge as a fitted line)
notes: Evaluate evidence of past and present movements of continental and oceanic crust and use plate tectonics to explain the ages of crustal rocks: oceanic crust gets older with distance from a mid-ocean ridge; North American continental crust gets younger away from an ancient central core. Rock ages come from radioactive decay (grade 10). Placed in Physics, not Biology as NGSS Appendix K places it, because it needs the plate model of this course and radiometric dating from grade 10; the high school reference units also place it in physics.

words: meteorite; impact crater; radiometric dating; solar system formation; 4.6 billion years; zircon
notes: Apply reasoning and evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites and other planetary surfaces to build an account of how Earth formed with the solar system about 4.6 billion years ago and what its early history was: absolute ages of meteorites, moon rocks and the oldest minerals from radiometric dating; sizes and make-up of solar system bodies; impact craters. Placed in Physics, not Biology as NGSS Appendix K places it, because it needs radiometric dating (grade 10) and the solar system and orbit models of this course. Teacher note: the age of the Earth is taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5).
